studies.title: They Ate Food And Walked
studies.meaning: An objection is answered by conceding it. The complaint was that a real messenger would not need meals or errands; the reply agrees that every earlier messenger ate and shopped, and denies that this proves anything. Then the frame widens without warning. The differences between people are themselves a mutual test, each person an examination set for the other. The question that follows is put to everyone, not only to the Prophet, and the section ends on watching rather than on judgement.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Surah 25 works through the objections raised against the message in Mecca, quoting them and answering in turn. The leaders had asked why no treasure was sent down to him, why no angel walked beside him, why he behaved like an ordinary trader. The commentators describe the general climate of mockery rather than reporting one occasion for this ayah. The community around the Prophet was small, poor and socially mixed, which sharpened the complaint.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word for a place where goods are driven together for sale. It carries haggling, dust and public visibility, which is exactly the ordinariness the objectors thought disqualified a messenger.

From a root meaning to smelt metal in order to separate it from its ore. The word covers testing, temptation and affliction at once, so what is described is a process that reveals rather than a punishment.
An intensive form from seeing. Placed after a test is announced, it says the examination is watched rather than left to itself, and it closes the ayah with attention instead of verdict.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca lived by trade, and the market was where standing became visible. Seasonal fairs at Ukaz and Dhul-Majaz drew poets and merchants from across the peninsula. A man of rank sent servants; a man without rank carried his own sack of dates and argued over the price himself. To be seen buying grain was to be publicly placed, and the objectors were pointing at exactly that.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about eating food and walking in the marketplaces is not new here. It appears earlier in the same surah, at ayah seven, as the objectors' own words of complaint. Thirteen ayat later the identical description is repeated as God's answer, so the accusation and the reply use the same sentence, with only the conclusion drawn from it reversed.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Prophethood is not a change of species. The messenger stays inside the ordinary conditions of hunger, commerce and fatigue, which is what makes the message reachable by the people receiving it. The second half establishes something further: social difference is not neutral scenery but part of the moral examination, and it runs both ways. The wealthy test the poor and the poor test the wealthy.

crossReferences.why: States the same principle about earlier messengers, adding that they were not bodies which did not eat food.
Shows the mutual test in action, as the comfortable ask whether God really favoured these poor believers.
Answers the same objection from the other side: had angels lived on earth, an angel would have been sent.

studies.applyIt: Pick one person today whose situation is very different from yours: someone who serves you, or someone whose life you envy. Consider that each of you is part of the other's examination, and that the same question is being put to you both. Then do one small thing that would look well if the whole arrangement were being watched, which the last words say it is.

studies.title: A God Made Of Wanting
studies.meaning: The idolatry described here has no shrine and no carved stone. What has been installed in the place of God is appetite: whatever a person finally wants decides what they do, and the decision is made before any argument arrives. That explains the second sentence. Hearing and reasoning are the two faculties an argument works on, and both have been given over. The comparison to grazing animals is exact rather than abusive, and it ends by saying the state is worse, since an animal follows instinct as it was made to.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has been recording what the leaders of Mecca said about the message, including their claim in the preceding ayah that they had patiently held to their own gods and nearly been talked out of them. This passage is the reply to that claim. The classical sources report several accounts naming particular Meccans, but they differ, so the general setting of open ridicule is the safer frame.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to fall or to plunge downward, used of air rushing into a void. The Arabic hears inclination as descent, so the word carries the direction of travel inside itself.
The one entrusted with another's affairs and answerable for them. Asking whether the Prophet would be this for such a person sets a limit on what preaching is responsible for.
Specifically camels, cattle, sheep and goats: the herded animals of that economy, not wild ones. The point is not stupidity but being led, moving where food and water lead without weighing anything.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Everyone listening had watched a herd move. Goats and camels went out at dawn behind whichever animal started walking, drifted toward water, and came back at dusk without a decision having been made by any of them. Herding was ordinary work, often given to boys. The comparison was not an insult borrowed from elsewhere. It was the most familiar picture of motion without judgement that the audience had.
studies.didYouKnow: The same comparison, in almost the same words, appears in Surah 7 at ayah 179, where it follows a description of hearts that do not understand, eyes that do not see and ears that do not hear. Both places end with the identical unexpected turn, that the state is further astray than the animals rather than merely equal to them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Idolatry is redefined from the outside in. It is not established by what stands in a temple but by what actually determines choices, which means it can exist in a person who owns no images and denies worshipping anything. The second ayah adds a limit that protects the messenger: he is not the guardian of anyone's response. Delivery is his charge, outcome is not.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same phrase about taking desire as a god, and adds sealed hearing and covered sight.
Gives the fuller version of the comparison, with the three faculties named that have stopped working.
States the limit directly: you are a reminder, and you are not set over them as a controller.

studies.applyIt: Name, privately, the one thing you would find hardest to give up. Then look back over the past week for a single decision that went against it. If you find one, that is useful information. If you cannot find one in a whole week, that is more useful still, and worth sitting with rather than explaining away.

studies.title: The Servants Of The Merciful
studies.meaning: This is a portrait, not a list of commands. It describes who certain people are, moving between public bearing and private hours: how they walk, how they answer provocation, what they do at night, what they fear, how they handle money, and finally the three wrongs they keep clear of. The word for their gait means manner rather than speed. The answer they give the ignorant is a single word that ends the exchange without conceding anything, which the commentators read as withdrawal rather than agreement.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from the later years before the emigration. The surah has spent sixty ayat on what the opponents of the message said and did. Here it turns and describes the other side instead. Those addressed as ignorant in the first line were not a hypothetical: believers in Mecca were insulted in the streets and in the assemblies, and the poorest among them had no clan strong enough to answer on their behalf.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning ease and lightness. It describes bearing rather than pace, so what is ruled out is the deliberate heavy walk of a man displaying his importance, not brisk movement.

A single word offered as a whole reply. The commentators read it as a formula of parting rather than of greeting here, a way of closing an exchange without either insulting back or pretending to agree.
From standing upright. The word names the point at which a thing holds its own weight, so the middle course between waste and stinginess is described as a structure rather than a compromise.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In Mecca a man's walk was read. The narrow lanes around the sanctuary were public, and swagger was cultivated as a claim to standing. Poetry prized the crushing reply, and the ability to answer an insult in kind was a genuine tribal asset that families cultivated in their young men. Refusing that exchange cost something visible, and it would have been noticed and discussed by everyone who saw it.
studies.didYouKnow: The description does not stop here. It continues to the end of the surah as a single grammatical chain, each clause hanging from the same opening phrase about the servants of the Merciful, roughly ten of them in a row. The surah therefore closes on one long sentence, whose subject is named once at the start and never repeated.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Three ayat earlier the objectors had asked what the Merciful even is, and refused to bow to a name they said they did not know. This passage answers that question by pointing at people rather than by defining a term. The divine name is explained through the character of those who serve under it, which places mercy in the visible world as behaviour before it is discussed as an attribute.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same instruction about bearing and gait, adding moderation of the voice, in a father's advice.
Pictures the balance in spending as a hand neither chained to the neck nor stretched wide open.
Shows the identical response to empty talk: turning away, and a farewell of peace to the ignorant.

studies.applyIt: The next time someone speaks to you with contempt, in a message thread or across a counter, answer with one short neutral sentence and then stop writing or talking. Do not explain the restraint afterwards to anyone. Notice what the silence costs you in the moment, and notice how much of that cost is still there an hour later.

studies.title: Except The One Who Turns
studies.meaning: Everything here turns on one word. The gravest wrongs have just been named, a doubled and lasting punishment is announced, and then the sentence is interrupted by an exception. Three things are asked for: turning back, believing, and repaired action, in that order. What follows is more than cancellation. Commentators differ over the exchange described: some read the record itself as rewritten, the old entries becoming good ones; others read it as a changed life, where the habit of the wrong is replaced by its opposite. Both readings are old.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The passage arrives immediately after the three wrongs listed at the close of the portrait of the servants of the Merciful. The classical sources preserve accounts of people who had killed or committed grave offences before Islam and feared no turning would be accepted for them, and connect this exception with that fear. The reports name different individuals and differ over the details, so the general situation is firmer than any single account.

keyTerms.note: A verb of physical return, used of a traveller reversing direction. The same root is used of God turning toward the person, so the movement is described from both sides with one word.
An intensive form meaning to put one thing in the place of another, not to remove and leave a gap. The wrong is not deleted here; something takes its position.
From lightness of weight, the opposite of being held in honour. The punishment described includes losing standing, which in the culture addressed was felt as sharply as pain.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A killing in tribal Arabia did not stay with the killer. It bound two families to vengeance or to a negotiated payment of camels, and the obligation outlived the men who incurred it. There was no procedure by which a person could privately settle such a thing and be finished with it. People arriving at the new community carried histories that their own society had offered them no way to close.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran describes forgiveness in several ways: wrongs remitted, wrongs covered, good deeds driving out bad ones. The particular image here, of bad deeds exchanged for good ones, is not repeated in these terms anywhere else in the text. It occurs once, at the point where the heaviest offences have just been listed by name.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Placing the opening immediately after the worst is deliberate: no category of wrong is set outside it, which is a claim about the reach of mercy rather than about the seriousness of the acts. The conditions attached matter too. Turning back is joined to belief and to work done afterwards, so what is described is a change in direction that shows up in behaviour, not a feeling recorded privately.

crossReferences.why: Addresses those who have wronged themselves without limit and forbids despair of God's mercy.
States the same movement briefly: whoever does wrong then asks God's pardon will find Him forgiving.
Gives the other image of the same process, good deeds driving away the bad ones.

studies.applyIt: Think of the one thing you would least want read aloud about yourself. Do not analyse it and do not resolve anything. Simply put it into a single sentence addressed to God, silently, tonight. Most people find the sentence harder to compose than they expected, and that difficulty is itself part of what the passage is describing.

studies.title: Coolness Of The Eyes
studies.meaning: The long portrait of the servants of the Merciful ends with a request, and its content is domestic. They ask for their spouses and children to be a joy to them. The phrase behind the English is an idiom of settled relief rather than excitement: in a hot country the tears of grief were felt as hot and the tears of relief as cool, so what is asked for is an eye that has stopped searching. The second half widens the request outward, asking to be a pattern others can follow.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. In Mecca the message divided households. A believing man might have a hostile wife, a believing woman a father determined to marry her elsewhere, and conversion could cost a person the protection of their own kin. Read in that setting, this is not the contentment of a settled family but a request made by people whose homes were the place the pressure was felt most sharply and most privately.

keyTerms.note: An old idiom for joy that has come to rest. Arab usage associated grief with hot tears and relief with cool ones, so the phrase names the end of anxious looking rather than excitement.
From standing in front. The word is singular although the speakers are plural, which commentators read either as one body asking together or as each asking to be such a person.
From a root meaning to guard oneself, originally shielding the body in a fight. The request is to lead people who are already careful, not to lead the careless.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Households in Mecca were extended and physically close: a compound of rooms around a shared court, several generations, unmarried relatives, servants. Sons were counted as economic and defensive strength, and a man's marriages tied him into the alliances of other clans. Family was therefore never only private. What happened in a house was known and weighed by the whole quarter within a day.
studies.didYouKnow: Of the roughly ten clauses describing the servants of the Merciful, only two are quoted prayers rather than descriptions of conduct. The first asks to be spared the fire. The second is this one, asking for a household and for a place among those worth imitating. The portrait therefore closes in the speakers' own voice rather than the narrator's.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Family life is placed inside devotion rather than beside it as a distraction from it. A description of night vigils and disciplined spending ends by asking God for joy in a spouse and children, with no sense of a change of subject. The second request adds something further: the ambition permitted here is to be worth copying, which is influence sought for the sake of the thing being copied.

crossReferences.why: Gives a matching prayer at forty, joining gratitude for parents to a request for good in one's offspring.
Shows Abraham asking the same way, for himself and his descendants together rather than for himself alone.
Records Zechariah asking for offspring in old age, and being answered while he stood praying.

studies.applyIt: This evening, say one specific true thing to someone in your household about something they actually did today. Not a general compliment and not a thank you for a chore. Something you noticed and they may not know you noticed. The passage asks for delight in these people, and delight starts with paying attention closely enough to have material.
